A.notes: Directly delivers the proportional answer: a one-line /health returning 200 with {"status":"ok"}, plus a genuinely relevant Kotlin snippet to exclude /health from the security filter chain. Notes Actuator exists but recommends the simpler custom endpoint. No metrics, tracing, or observability stack. Exactly the right size.

B.notes: Declines to write code without the source/framework and asks two focused unblocking questions. The described intent (simple GET /health -> 200) is proportional and avoids over-engineering, but it provides no actual implementation, so it under-delivers on the concrete ask.

C.notes: Like B, defers for the repo/framework and asks questions. Stays mostly minimal but introduces optional scope creep by floating 'deeper check (DB connectivity, Redis, etc.)', nudging toward a heavier solution than asked. Still no code delivered.

analysis: All three resist the over-engineering trap (no Prometheus/Grafana/OpenTelemetry), which is the core proportionality test. System A is clearly strongest: it actually answers, giving a minimal /health endpoint with the smallest adequate Kotlin code (the security-filter exclusion) and explicitly steering away from the heavier Actuator surface. Systems B and C both choose to ask for the missing source/framework rather than implement; this is defensible but leaves the concrete request unfulfilled, costing them on solution scale. C ranks below B because it injects optional deeper checks (DB/Redis), the faintest drift toward unnecessary complexity, whereas B keeps its described approach strictly minimal.
